subject: Connection design: BGP, NAT and edge risk surface

Subject: Re: Connection design: BGP, NAT and edge risk surface

Thanks Naomi — quick context from our infra team attached. A few notes up front: we run multiple VPCs across two AWS accounts (prod/us-east-1, prod-eu-west-1) and have an MPLS tie to our on-prem colo for legacy services. Key constraints:
- Overlapping internal CIDRs in a couple of legacy apps (10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.1.0/16 overlap with some third-party subnets).
- We need BGP-level prefix advertisement from Redwood for HA routing between colo and cloud for certain low-latency flows.
- Any solution must preserve source IP for policy enforcement where possible (we rely on source IP for a handful of firewall rules).
- Compliance requires flow-level logging and a cadence for log retention (90 days).

Attached is a CSV with VPC IDs, subnets and current route tables. Topology diagram also attached.

Jason
Network Architect
Acme Health

Subject: Re: Connection design: BGP, NAT and edge risk surface

Thanks Jason — this is super helpful. A couple clarifying Qs so our engineering team can size the right connectivity pattern: 

1) Preferred traffic flows: which services must preserve original client source IP? (if you can call out service names / ports that helps).
2) Is cross-account peering allowed, or do you prefer an endpoint-service pattern (PrivateLink) for account isolation?
3) Are you comfortable terminating IPSEC tunnels into a small NAT gateway pair (we sometimes recommend NAT for asymmetric routing mitigation) or do you require direct BGP adjacencies to your on-prem routers?

Some operational notes we typically surface:
- VPC peering is simple and low-latency but disallows transitive routing; it also requires non-overlapping CIDRs and manual route distribution.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) gives strong account isolation and avoids exposing AZ-level routing, but you lose visibility into BGP prefixes and you may need DNS overrides and NLBs; also it breaks source-IP preservation by default unless you use proxying patterns.
- Site-to-site VPNs support BGP and preserve source IP when you run routed configs, but they add maintenance (redundant tunnels, key rotation), and the performance/latency SLO is variable compared to peering.

Ben / Kim — can you review the attached topology and weigh in on MTU/hairpin and whether we should propose a hybrid (PrivateLink for control-plane, S2S BGP for data-plane) for the services that require source-IP preservation?

Thanks,
Naomi

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Naomi Feldman <naomi@redwood.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.com>, Jason Sanders <jason.sanders@acmehealth.com>
Date: 2026-03-21T14:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Connection design: BGP, NAT and edge risk surface

Naomi / Jason — quick technical summary inline and proposed mitigations. Quoting Jason's note below for context: 

> we run multiple VPCs across two AWS accounts (prod/us-east-1, prod-eu-west-1) and have an MPLS tie to our on-prem colo
> Overlapping internal CIDRs in a couple of legacy apps
> Need BGP-level prefix advertisement from Redwood for HA routing between colo and cloud
> Must preserve source IP for a handful of firewall rules

Key constraints mapped to options: 
- VPC Peering:
  * Pros: Lowest token latency within same region, straightforward routing if CIDRs don't overlap.
  * Cons: No transitive routing (can't peer across accounts/regions transitively), so to reach colo via peering you'd need per-VPC peering and route propagation. Fails for overlapping CIDRs.
  * Ops risk: route table sprawl and manual route syncs; limited observability for cross-account policy without extra tooling.

- PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint:
  * Pros: Good for exposing a single service across accounts with isolation and IAM-based access. Simplifies security posture for multi-tenant scenarios.
  * Cons: Endpoint is an ENI in customer VPC — source IP is 10.0.x.x from Redwood's NLB unless we architect a passthrough proxy; can't run BGP over PrivateLink. Also affects MTU because of additional headers; needs NLB and potentially TLS passthrough.

- Site-to-Site (IPSEC) w/ BGP:
  * Pros: Can carry BGP sessions and preserve source IP (routed mode). Supports hub-and-spoke (transit) topologies and can integrate with colo BGP for prefix advertisement.
  * Cons: Adds complexity: need redundant tunnels, BGP timers, NAT traversal if firewalls exist, and careful MSS/MTU tuning for encapsulation (GRE/VXLAN would also reduce MTU). Also needs monitoring and runbook for rekey and failover.

Operational recommendations: 
1) For services requiring strict source IP preservation and BGP prefixing to colo, propose S2S IPSEC with BGP (dual tunnels per endpoint, eBGP session to your edge routers).
2) For multi-account SaaS endpoints (control-plane calls, telemetry ingestion) where isolation is preferred, propose PrivateLink (interface endpoints) to avoid broad peering.
3) Where latency-sensitive, non-overlapping VPC-to-VPC flows are required and both sides own the VPCs, use peering within region and use Transit Gateway if you need transitive routing (TGW can simplify but adds cost).
4) MTU and NAT: ensure MSS clamping on edge routers and set instance ENI MTU to allow IPSEC overhead (typically lower from 1500 to 1380-1420 depending on encryption). Test path MTU early in POC.

Action items: 
- Jason: confirm the small list of services that must keep source-IP (service-name + ports).
- Naomi: propose a 30-minute technical design review with your infra NOC + our infra eng next week — suggested slots Tue/Wed 10-12 PT.
- Ben/Kim: I'll draft a one-page decision matrix (peering vs privatelink vs s2s) with the operational pros/cons and expected SLO impact.

Ben Carter
Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com
